mcq.explanation: Ingress defines HTTP/HTTPS routing rules to Services: host names and URL paths map to backend Services, optionally with TLS.
mcq.distractors: Branch protection, CPU architecture and build steps are not Kubernetes networking concerns.

mcq.explanation: An Ingress controller (e.g. Traefik, HAProxy, NGINX, or a cloud controller like AWS Load Balancer Controller) is needed: an Ingress object is only configuration, and nothing routes traffic until a controller watches it and programs a proxy.
mcq.distractors: Git tags, Terraform lock files and registries play no part in routing traffic.

mcq.explanation: A ConfigMap is for non-sensitive configuration data such as feature flags, URLs or config files, stored as plain key/value pairs.
mcq.distractors: Passwords belong in Secrets, disks in PersistentVolumes, and images in registries.

mcq.explanation: A Secret stores sensitive configuration values (passwords, tokens, keys, TLS certificates). It is kept separate so RBAC, encryption at rest and external secret managers can protect it.
mcq.distractors: Images live in registries, logs go to a logging stack, and Helm binaries are not stored in the cluster.

mcq.explanation: A Pod can consume a ConfigMap as environment variables (`env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` or `envFrom.configMapRef`) or as mounted files via a `configMap` volume. Mounted files update when the ConfigMap changes; env vars only change when the Pod restarts.
mcq.distractors: Kernel flags, build cache and commit messages are not ways Pods read configuration.

mcq.explanation: An Ingress path rule matches the HTTP request path (e.g. `/api`), with `pathType` Prefix, Exact or ImplementationSpecific deciding how it matches.
mcq.distractors: It is unrelated to filesystem, mount or Git paths.

mcq.explanation: TLS termination at the Ingress provides HTTPS encryption for client connections: the controller presents the certificate from a TLS Secret, decrypts the traffic, and usually forwards plain HTTP to the Services.
mcq.distractors: Autoscaling, volumes and artifact signing are separate features.

mcq.explanation: `kubectl get configmaps` (short `cm`) lists ConfigMaps in the namespace.
mcq.distractors: `secrets-only`, `networks` and `charts` are not Kubernetes resource types.

mcq.explanation: No: base64 is encoding rather than encryption. Anyone who can read the Secret can decode it with `base64 -d`. Real protection comes from RBAC, encryption at rest for etcd (EncryptionConfiguration/KMS) and external secret managers.
mcq.distractors: Base64 is not encryption or hashing, and Secrets can hold any string or binary data.

mcq.explanation: A Secret of type `kubernetes.io/tls` (keys `tls.crt` and `tls.key`) holds the certificate and key, referenced from the Ingress `spec.tls[].secretName`.
mcq.distractors: ConfigMaps are for non-sensitive data, Deployments run Pods, and ServiceAccounts are identities.

checks.label: Defines an Ingress (kind: Ingress / kubectl create ingress)

labs.modelAnswer:
# Prerequisite: an Ingress controller, e.g. `minikube addons enable ingress` or Traefik via Helm
kubectl get ingressclass                     # note the class name (nginx / traefik ...)

kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80
kubectl create deployment api --image=hashicorp/http-echo:1.0 -- /http-echo -text=api -listen=:5678
kubectl expose deployment api --port=80 --target-port=5678

# ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: demo
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx            # use your controller's class
  rules:
    - host: demo.local
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api
                port:
                  number: 80
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web
                port:
                  number: 80

kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml
kubectl get ingress demo                     # ADDRESS filled in by the controller
kubectl describe ingress demo                # rules and backends with endpoints
curl -H "Host: demo.local" http://<ingress-ip>/api   # -> api
curl -H "Host: demo.local" http://<ingress-ip>/      # -> nginx welcome page
labs.explanation: Tests that you can route HTTP traffic by host and path to different Services. Verify an Ingress controller is running and the Ingress uses its class, that each path points at an existing Service and port, and that curl with the right Host header reaches the expected backend. The upstream ingress-nginx project was retired in 2026, so new clusters often use another controller or the Gateway API, but the Ingress resource itself is unchanged.

checks.label: Injects it as env vars (configMapRef / configMapKeyRef)
Checks values inside a Pod (kubectl exec ... printenv/env)

labs.modelAnswer:
kubectl create configmap app-config \
  --from-literal=APP_MODE=production \
  --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info
kubectl get configmap app-config -o yaml

# deploy.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: app
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: app-config          # all keys become env vars
          env:
            - name: MODE                  # or pick a single key
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: app-config
                  key: APP_MODE

kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
kubectl rollout status deployment/app
kubectl exec deploy/app -- printenv APP_MODE LOG_LEVEL MODE
# production
# info
# production
labs.explanation: Tests decoupling configuration from the image with a ConfigMap. Verify the ConfigMap keys show up as environment variables inside the running container. Remember env vars are read at container start: after changing the ConfigMap you must restart the Pods (`kubectl rollout restart deployment/app`) to see new values.

checks.label: Creates a Secret (kubectl create secret / kind: Secret)
References it from the workload (secretKeyRef / secretRef / secret volume)
Verifies the Pod received it (kubectl exec / logs)

labs.modelAnswer:
# Credential comes from a local file, not the manifest (and not shell history)
printf 'app_user' > ./username.txt
printf '<generate-a-random-password>' > ./password.txt
kubectl create secret generic db-cred \
  --from-file=username=./username.txt \
  --from-file=password=./password.txt
rm ./username.txt ./password.txt
kubectl get secret db-cred            # TYPE Opaque, DATA 2 (values not shown)

# pod.yaml - contains only a reference to the Secret
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]
      env:
        - name: DB_USER
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: db-cred
              key: username
      volumeMounts:
        - name: creds
          mountPath: /etc/creds
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: creds
      secret:
        secretName: db-cred

kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
kubectl exec app -- printenv DB_USER          # app_user
kubectl exec app -- ls /etc/creds             # password  username
labs.explanation: Tests consuming a credential through a Secret reference so the value never appears in the Deployment/Pod manifest. Check that the manifest only names the Secret and key, that the value is created from a file, env file or external secret manager, and that the Pod can see it as an env var or mounted file. Avoid printing the real password as evidence, and remember base64 in a Secret YAML is not encryption.
